subject: FluxBio committed capacity: burst allocation & SLO-fit recommendation
messages:
From: Liam Ortiz <liam.ortiz@fluxbio.com>
To: hannah_schmitt@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-11-02T09:14:00-08:00
Subject: Sizing ask — committed capacity + burst guarantees

Hi Hannah,

Thanks for taking this — small follow up from our side. Our product team drove an early performance sweep against the ensemble we expect to run in prod (roughly: 8k prompt tokens plus 512 token generation on average, model family is an open-weights 34B variant). Typical steady-state is ~700 tokens/sec, but we see short bursts up to ~2.6k tokens/sec for 90s during peak user flows.

Two asks:
- Can you map those numbers to committed slabs (we prefer 4-GPU slabs) and show p95 latency fit for a 1.2s generation SLO?
- What's the recommended safety/headroom multiplier you would advise for EU region (we care about predictable tail latency and want to avoid fallback for 99.9% of bursts)?

Happy to share more telemetry if you need it — attaching our token distribution CSV.

Thanks,
Liam
Senior Engineering Manager, FluxBio
[attachment: fluxbio-token-profile.csv (text/csv)]

From: hannah_schmitt@redwood.ai
To: Liam Ortiz <liam.ortiz@fluxbio.com>
Cc: ben_carter@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-11-02T11:02:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Sizing ask — committed capacity + burst guarantees

Thanks Liam — got the CSV and the burst screenshot. Preliminary pass below; I'll pull Karthik in for kernel/latency specifics. High-level summary:

Observation summary (quick):
- Steady tokens/sec: 700 t/s average.
- Observed short bursts: up to 2,600 t/s for ~60-120s windows.
- Target p95 SLO: generation latency <= 1.2s for the typical 512-token tail piece.

Quick model mapping assumptions:
- Benchmark target: open-34B quantized to 8-bit (production profiling shows ~580 t/s per A100-80GB with the current runtime profile when using continuous batching and warmed KV cache; using H100 would improve raw throughput ~1.6x but availability/price in EU matters).
- For safety math below we use a conservative per-GPU throughput of 500 t/s to account for mixed-length tails and modest off-host noise.

Sizing math (conservative):
- Peak burst requirement: 2,600 t/s.
- Required GPUs (raw) = ceil(2600 / 500) = 6 GPUs.
- Slab definition = 4 GPUs per slab -> minimum slabs to serve peak without queuing = ceil(6 / 4) = 2 slabs (8 GPUs).

Headroom and SLO fit:
- With 8 GPUs at 500 t/s assumed, we get 4,000 t/s capacity. That implies a headroom factor = 4,000 / 2,600 ≈ 1.54x on the observed burst.
- Empirical p95 latency on the benchmarked profile at 500 t/s/GPU => p95 generation ≈ 0.9s for 512-token tail when KV cache is warm and batching is effective. Conservatively, add 20% network/queueing allowance -> ~1.1s p95.

Recommendation (short):
- Commit 2 slabs (8 GPUs A100-80GB equivalent) in EU to meet bursts with ~1.5x headroom.
- Add a soft burst reserve (hosted burst capacity) of 1 additional slab for temporary spikes during product launches (pay-as-you-go).

I'll follow up with Karthik on latency tail sources and a variant that uses H100-equivalent pricing to see if we can reduce GPU count while staying within SLO.

Next step: schedule a 30-min runthrough tomorrow — I can share the math workbook.

— Hannah
Hannah Schmitt | Principal Solutions 
Redwood Inference

Liam / team — quick operational note from ops side:
- Thermal and autoscaler behavior for EU zones means a hard dependency on our spot/burst inventory; committing 2 slabs gives strong predictability but our recommended contract (to avoid forced fallbacks) is commit + a 1-slab burst buffer available on-demand for a 6-month launch window.
- Also recommend we instrument synthetic burst canaries (30s every 4 hours) to validate p95 during production traffic.

Ben
Head of Dedicated Ops, Redwood

On the math workbook: I'll add a tab with our autoscaler-trigger threshold and a plan for proactive pre-warming during expected launch windows.

From: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
To: ben_carter@redwood.ai, hannah_schmitt@redwood.ai, Liam Ortiz <liam.ortiz@fluxbio.com>
Date: 2026-11-03T10:45:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Sizing ask — committed capacity + burst guarantees

Adding a micro-benchmarked run and some latency caveats:
- We ran the ensemble config against a 34B-family checkpoint quantized to 8-bit across A100-80GB (single-GPU numbers): avg sustained throughput ~520 t/s with aggressive batching (8 concurrent streams), p95 single-shot generation for 512 tokens ~0.78s when KV cache is warm.
- Cold-start and multi-tenant jitter can reduce per-GPU effective throughput to ~420 t/s. That’s why Hannah used 500 t/s as a conservative midpoint.

Alternative: H100-equivalent pricing (or inference-optimized instances) can push per-GPU to ~820 t/s in our tests, which would reduce slab requirement to 1 slab + 1 on-demand slab for bursts. Tradeoffs: higher hourly cost, more limited capacity in EU.

Operationally suggested configuration:
- Primary: 2 committed slabs (8 GPUs) on A100-equivalent with 1.5x headroom.
- Optional opt-in: H100-backed 1-slab reserved reserve for sustained acceleration (if FluxBio prefers fewer GPUs over cost).

I'll attach the micro-benchmark outputs to the Drive folder.

— Karthik
Applied ML / Inference Performance

Appreciate the detailed math and options — this is very helpful. A few clarifying Qs before the call:
1) If we commit 2 slabs (8 GPUs) plus 1 on-demand slab, what would the expected monthly committed spend look like vs an H100-lean option? Please put both as a delta to our expected ARR contribution.
2) For the p95 numbers you quoted, what percent of user flows still hit fallback for 99.9%? Our compliance team wants >99.5% success without fallback during launch windows.

We'll convene product and finance before the call and come prepared with an acceptable spend delta.

Thanks — Liam

From: hannah_schmitt@redwood.ai
To: Liam Ortiz <liam.ortiz@fluxbio.com>
Cc: ben_carter@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, jordan_blake@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-11-05T16:33:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Sizing ask — committed capacity + burst guarantees

Liam — answering Qs and next steps:
1) Cost delta (high level):
   - 2 slabs committed (8x A100-equivalent) + 1 on-demand slab for bursts -> baseline committed monthly = approximately EUR 92k/month (this factors host, support, and reserved pricing). On-demand slab usage during launch windows estimated additional EUR 12-22k depending on hours consumed.
   - H100-lean option (1 committed slab H100-equivalent + 1 on-demand H100 slab) -> committed monthly ≈ EUR 110k/month but reduces expected GPU count and unit hours; net TCO may be comparable depending on burst frequency. I'll add a formal cost comparison table in the workbook.

2) p99.9 / fallback likelihood:
   - With the conservative 500 t/s/GPU assumption and 2 committed slabs + 1 on-demand slab, our simulations show >99.6% of bursts complete without fallback during observed burst distributions (assuming pre-warm request routing and synthetic canaries enabled). Reaching >99.9% would require either an additional committed slab or a more aggressive warm-burst reserve policy.

Recommended next steps:
- Quick pricing appendix: Hannah + Jordan to add a cost delta sheet and run a 3-month P&L projection against expected ARR.
- Ops runbook: Ben to add synthetic canaries + autoscaler thresholds.
- Customer decision: FluxBio to confirm whether they prefer committed-cost-minimizing (A100) or committed-GPU-minimizing (H100) approach.

I'll lock in a 30-min slot for Friday 09:00 CET to walk through the workbook and finalize the recommended commit. Please ping if you want earlier.

— Hannah
Principal Solutions, Redwood Inference
